From 1970 - 1974, however, there was a complete reversal of a 150-year trend during which big cities and suburbs grew faster than rural areas. During the 1960's the population of metropolitan areas rose four times as fast as counties beyond their borders. Between 1970 and 1974, metropolitan areas gained 3.4 percent in population. Small cities and rural areas gained 5.5 percent. New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, and Detroit all lost population. Some new fast-growing areas are places with long records of declining economies and population. FORTUNE notes that (a) the lure of the boondocks is remarkably strong among people living in metropolitan areas, (b) this causes a high potential for redistribution of everything, and (c) this could reshape the life-style and business map of the entire Nation, and that this means the distinctions between central cities and outer suburbs will gradually fade away. 33/
With several large cities losing population it is interesting to note that an author concludes in a 1975 book that under continued economic non-growth, metropolitan areas become extremely resistant to decline in population. 34/
A 1974 report to Congress stated that in the 20 years prior to 1970, urbanized land almost tripled to 35,000 square miles. 35/ A forecast by the Commission on Urban Problems states that by the year 2000 an additional 18 million acres of land will come into urban use for the first time. 36/ This would mean that the amount of land in urban use would almost double from 1970-2000. Urbanized Areas include suburbs of minimum population densities.
The U.S. Bureau of the Census anticipates that between 1976 and 1990 the total number of households will increase by 31 percent. The land-consuming, one-family house is still the kind of home most workers want. Polls indicate many will make whatever sacrifices are necessary to get one. 37/
Research on the transportation outlook for the year 2000 stated:
"Although retail and service industries, which are closely tied to the residential market, have moved to the suburbs, the fastest growing categories of service-industry, management, government, advertising, administration, education - more generally communications industries - show a strong tendency to locate in the core.

. . . If the urban core were easily accessable (convenient and 20 minutes or less away) . . . the urban core would grow to become a vital city of activity involving those types of highly specialized services which cannot survive in a suburban plaza.
